thm-7-1-1.tex:
\leanmarker{thm-7-1-1}{Theorem 7.1.1} A complete lattice \(L\) is continuous if and only if, for every family \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) of directed subsets of \(L\),
\[
  \bigwedge_{i\in I}\bigvee{}^{\uparrow} A_i
  =
  \bigvee_{f:I\overset{\odot}{\longrightarrow}\bigcup_i A_i}^{\uparrow}
    \bigwedge_{i\in I} f(i).
\]

def-7-1-2.tex:
\leanmarker{def-7-1-2}{Definition 7.1.2} For a complete lattice \(L\), define \(x \lll y\) by
\[
  x \lll y \quad\text{iff}\quad
  \forall A\subseteq L,\ \bigl(y\le \bigvee A \Rightarrow \exists a\in A,\ x\le a\bigr).
\]
The lattice \(L\) is prime-continuous if \(x=\bigvee\{y\mid y\lll x\}\) for every \(x\in L\).

thm-7-1-3.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-1-3}{Theorem 7.1.3} A complete lattice is prime-continuous if and only if it is completely distributive.

def-7-1-4.tex:
\leanmarker{def-7-1-4}{Definition 7.1.4} A complete lattice \(L\) is \(\wedge\)-generated by a subset \(A\) if, for every \(x\in L\),
\[
  x = \bigwedge(\uparrow x\cap A).
\]
Dually, one speaks of \(\vee\)-generation.

def-7-1-5.tex: \leanmarker{def-7-1-5}{Definition 7.1.5} An element \(x\) of a lattice \(L\) is \(\wedge\)-irreducible if \(x=\bigwedge M\) for a finite set \(M\subseteq L\) implies \(x=m\) for some \(m\in M\). It is \(\wedge\)-prime if \(x\ge \bigwedge M\) implies \(x\ge m\) for some \(m\in M\), again for finite \(M\). Allowing arbitrary \(M\subseteq L\) gives the completely \(\wedge\)-irreducible and completely \(\wedge\)-prime notions; the dual notions exchange suprema and infima.

prop-7-1-6.tex: \leanmarker{prop-7-1-6}{Proposition 7.1.6} A \(\wedge\)-prime element is also \(\wedge\)-irreducible. The converse holds if the lattice is distributive.

thm-7-1-7.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-1-7}{Theorem 7.1.7} A continuous lattice is \(\wedge\)-generated by its set of \(\wedge\)-irreducible elements; an algebraic lattice is \(\wedge\)-generated by its completely \(\wedge\)-irreducible elements. The proof separates \(x\nleq y\) by a Scott-open filter and then applies Zorn's lemma to a maximal element above \(y\) outside the filter.

thm-7-1-8.tex:
\leanmarker{thm-7-1-8}{Theorem 7.1.8} If \(L\) is a complete lattice which is \(\wedge\)-generated by \(\wedge\)-prime elements, then \(L\) satisfies
\[
  \bigwedge_{m\in M}\bigvee A_m
  =
  \bigvee_{f:M\overset{\odot}{\longrightarrow}\bigcup_m A_m}
    \bigwedge_{m\in M} f(m)
\]
for finite \(M\), and
\[
  \bigvee_{i\in I}\bigwedge M_i
  =
  \bigwedge_{f:I\overset{\odot}{\longrightarrow}\bigcup_i M_i}
    \bigvee_{i\in I} f(i)
\]
when the sets \(M_i\) are finite.

def-7-1-9.tex: \leanmarker{def-7-1-9}{Definition 7.1.9} A frame-homomorphism between complete lattices \(K\) and \(L\) is a map preserving arbitrary suprema and finite infima.

def-7-1-10.tex: \leanmarker{def-7-1-10}{Definition 7.1.10} A filter \(F\subseteq L\) is prime if \(M\in F\) implies \(F\cap M\ne\emptyset\) for every finite \(M\subseteq L\). Allowing arbitrary \(M\) gives completely prime filters. Dually, one has completely prime ideals.

prop-7-1-11.tex: \leanmarker{prop-7-1-11}{Proposition 7.1.11} For a complete lattice \(L\) and subset \(F\subseteq L\), the following are equivalent: \(F\) is a completely prime filter; \(F\) is a filter and \(L\setminus F=\downarrow x\) for some \(x\in L\); \(L\setminus F=\downarrow x\) for a \(\wedge\)-prime element \(x\); and \(\chi_F:L\to \mathbf{2}\) is a frame-homomorphism.

def-7-1-12.tex:
\leanmarker{def-7-1-12}{Definition 7.1.12} Let \(L\) be a complete lattice. The points of \(L\) are the completely prime filters of \(L\). The collection \(\operatorname{pt}(L)\) is topologized by the basic opens
\[
  O_x = \{F\in\operatorname{pt}(L)\mid x\in F\},\qquad x\in L.
\]

prop-7-1-13.tex:
\leanmarker{prop-7-1-13}{Proposition 7.1.13} The sets \(O_x\), \(x\in L\), form a topology on \(\operatorname{pt}(L)\). Indeed, for finite \(M\),
\[
  \bigcap_{m\in M} O_{x_m}=O_{\bigwedge_{m\in M}x_m},
\]
and for arbitrary \(I\),
\[
  \bigcup_{i\in I} O_{x_i}=O_{\bigvee_{i\in I}x_i},
\]
using that points are filters and completely prime filters.

thm-7-1-14.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-1-14}{Theorem 7.1.14} The functors \(\Omega:\mathbf{Top}\to\mathbf{CLat}\) and \(\operatorname{pt}:\mathbf{CLat}\to\mathbf{Top}\) are dual adjoints. The units are \(\eta\) and \(\epsilon\).

def-7-2-1.tex: \leanmarker{def-7-2-1}{Definition 7.2.1} A closed subset of a topological space is irreducible if it is non-empty and cannot be written as the union of two closed proper subsets.

prop-7-2-2.tex: \leanmarker{prop-7-2-2}{Proposition 7.2.2} For a topological space \(X\), the unit \(\eta_X:X\to\operatorname{pt}(\Omega(X))\) is injective iff \(X\) is \(T_0\), and it is surjective iff every irreducible closed set is the closure of a point of \(X\).

def-7-2-3.tex: \leanmarker{def-7-2-3}{Definition 7.2.3} A topological space \(X\) is sober if \(\eta_X\) is bijective. Equivalently, \(X\) is \(T_0\) and every irreducible closed set is the closure of a unique point.

prop-7-2-4.tex: \leanmarker{prop-7-2-4}{Proposition 7.2.4} For any complete lattice \(L\), the unit \(\epsilon_L:L\to\Omega(\operatorname{pt}(L))\) is surjective and monotone. Moreover, injectivity of \(\epsilon_L\), separation of elements of \(L\) by completely prime filters, and \(\wedge\)-generation of \(L\) by \(\wedge\)-prime elements are equivalent.

def-7-2-5.tex: \leanmarker{def-7-2-5}{Definition 7.2.5} A complete lattice \(L\) is spatial if \(\epsilon_L\) is bijective.

thm-7-2-6.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-2-6}{Theorem 7.2.6} A spatial lattice is a frame; in particular it is distributive.

thm-7-2-7.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-2-7}{Theorem 7.2.7} For every complete lattice \(L\), the space \(\operatorname{pt}(L)\) is sober. For every topological space \(X\), the lattice \(\Omega(X)\) is spatial.

cor-7-2-8.tex: \leanmarker{cor-7-2-8}{Corollary 7.2.8} The functors \(\Omega\) and \(\operatorname{pt}\) form a dual equivalence between sober spaces and spatial lattices.

thm-7-2-9.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-2-9}{Theorem 7.2.9} Let \(X\) be sober. The sets of open neighborhoods of compact saturated sets are precisely the Scott-open filters in \(\Omega(X)\).

cor-7-2-10.tex: \leanmarker{cor-7-2-10}{Corollary 7.2.10} For a sober space \(X\), the poset of compact saturated subsets ordered by inclusion is dually isomorphic to the poset of Scott-open filters in \(\Omega(X)\), also ordered by inclusion.

cor-7-2-11.tex: \leanmarker{cor-7-2-11}{Corollary 7.2.11} In a sober space, filtered intersections of compact saturated subsets are compact; non-empty filtered intersections of non-empty compact saturated subsets are non-empty. If such an intersection is contained in an open set \(O\), then some member of the family is already contained in \(O\).

prop-7-2-12.tex: \leanmarker{prop-7-2-12}{Proposition 7.2.12} For a \(T_0\)-space \(X\), the topology on \(X\) is finer than the weak upper topology induced by the specialization order.

prop-7-2-13.tex: \leanmarker{prop-7-2-13}{Proposition 7.2.13} A sober space is a dcpo in its specialization order, and its topology is coarser than the Scott topology induced by that order.

thm-7-2-14.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-2-14}{Theorem 7.2.14} The category of sober spaces is complete and cocomplete, and it is closed under retracts formed in the ambient category \(\mathbf{Top}\).

thm-7-2-16.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-2-16}{Theorem 7.2.16} The functors \(\Omega\) and \(\operatorname{pt}\) restrict to a dual equivalence between sober locally compact spaces and distributive continuous lattices.

def-7-2-17.tex: \leanmarker{def-7-2-17}{Definition 7.2.17} A topological space is coherent if it is sober, locally compact, and the intersection of two compact saturated subsets is compact.

def-7-2-18.tex: \leanmarker{def-7-2-18}{Definition 7.2.18} The order of approximation on a complete lattice is multiplicative if \(x\ll y\) and \(x\ll z\) imply \(x\ll y\wedge z\). A distributive continuous lattice with multiplicative approximation is arithmetic.

thm-7-2-19.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-2-19}{Theorem 7.2.19} The functors \(\Omega\) and \(\operatorname{pt}\) restrict to a dual equivalence between coherent spaces and arithmetic lattices.

thm-7-2-20.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-2-20}{Theorem 7.2.20} The functors \(\Omega\) and \(\operatorname{pt}\) restrict to a dual equivalence between sober spaces whose points have fundamental systems of compact-open neighborhoods and distributive algebraic lattices.

def-7-2-21.tex: \leanmarker{def-7-2-21}{Definition 7.2.21} A spectral space is a coherent space in which every point has a fundamental system of compact-open neighborhoods.

thm-7-2-22.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-2-22}{Theorem 7.2.22} The functors \(\Omega\) and \(\operatorname{pt}\) restrict to a dual equivalence between spectral spaces and algebraic arithmetic lattices.

prop-7-2-23.tex: \leanmarker{prop-7-2-23}{Proposition 7.2.23} If \(L\) is an algebraic arithmetic lattice, then completely prime filters of \(L\) correspond bijectively to prime filters of \(K(L)\). The topology on \(\operatorname{pt}(L)\) is generated by the opens \(O_x\) with \(x\in K(L)\).

def-7-2-24.tex:
\leanmarker{def-7-2-24}{Definition 7.2.24} A relation \(R\) between lattices \(V\) and \(W\) is join-approximable if:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1.\;& \forall x,x'\in V\ \forall y,y'\in W,\ (x'\ge x\ R\ y\ge y' \Rightarrow x'\ R\ y'),\\[2mm]
2.\;& \forall x\in V\ \forall N\subseteq_{\rm fin} W,\ (\forall y\in N,\ x\ R\ y \Rightarrow x\ R\bigvee N),\\[2mm]
3.\;& \forall M\subseteq_{\rm fin} V\ \forall y\in W,\ (\forall x\in M,\ x\ R\ y \Rightarrow (\bigwedge M)\ R\ y),\\[2mm]
4.\;& \forall M\subseteq_{\rm fin} V\ \forall x\in W,\ (\bigvee M)\ R\ x \Rightarrow \exists N\subseteq_{\rm fin} W,\\
& \qquad x=\bigvee N\ \wedge\ \forall n\in N\ \exists m\in M,\ m\ R\ n.
\end{aligned}
\]

prop-7-2-25.tex: \leanmarker{prop-7-2-25}{Proposition 7.2.25} Algebraic arithmetic lattices with frame-homomorphisms are equivalent to distributive lattices with join-approximable relations.

thm-7-2-26.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-2-26}{Theorem 7.2.26} Spectral spaces and continuous functions are dually equivalent to distributive lattices and join-approximable relations via the contravariant functors \(K\Omega\) and \(\operatorname{spec}\).

prop-7-2-27.tex:
\leanmarker{prop-7-2-27}{Proposition 7.2.27} Continuous domains equipped with the Scott topology are sober spaces.

\textit{Proof.} Let \(A\) be an irreducible closed set in a continuous domain \(D\), and put \(B=\downarrow A\). The set \(B\) is directed: if \(x,y\in B\), then neither \(D\setminus\uparrow x\) nor \(D\setminus\uparrow y\) contains all of \(A\), and irreducibility yields \(a\in A\cap\uparrow x\cap\uparrow y\). Since \(\uparrow x\cap\uparrow y\) is Scott-open, some \(b\ll a\) also lies in it, giving an upper bound for \(x\) and \(y\). Proposition 2.2.10 then shows that \(A\) is the closure of \(\bigvee{}^{\uparrow}B\).

thm-7-2-28.tex:
\leanmarker{thm-7-2-28}{Theorem 7.2.28} The functors \(\Omega\) and \(\operatorname{pt}\) restrict to a dual equivalence between \(\mathbf{CONT}\) and the category of completely distributive lattices.

\textit{Proof sketch.} A Scott-open set \(O\) in a continuous domain \(D\) is the union of the sets \(\uparrow x\), \(x\in O\), and each satisfies \(\uparrow x\lll O\) in \(\sigma D\); complete distributivity follows from Theorem 7.1.3. Conversely, if \(L\) is completely distributive, the points of \(L\), ordered by inclusion of filters, form a dcpo. Every completely prime filter \(F\) is enough approximants: whenever \(x\in F\), prime-continuity gives
\[
  x=\bigvee\{y\mid y\lll x\},
\]
so some \(y\in F\) satisfies \(y\lll x\). Interpolation gives a chain \(y\lll\cdots\lll y_n\lll\cdots\lll y_1\lll x\), and \(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\uparrow y_n\) is a completely prime filter containing \(x\) with infimum in \(F\). Thus \(F'\ll F\) iff \(\bigwedge F'\in F\). The Scott topology on the dcpo of points is then exactly the point topology, with basic opens \(O_x=\{F\mid x\in F\}\).

thm-7-2-29.tex:
\leanmarker{thm-7-2-29}{Theorem 7.2.29} The dual equivalence of Theorem 7.2.26 cuts down to a dual equivalence of coherent algebraic domains and lattices in which every element is the join of finitely many \(\vee\)-primes.

\textit{Proof sketch.} A compact-open set in an algebraic domain \(D\) is a finite union of sets of the form \(\uparrow c\) with \(c\in K(D)\), and these are characterized by being \(\vee\)-irreducible and \(\vee\)-prime. Conversely, if every element of a lattice is a finite join of \(\vee\)-primes, then its ideal completion is completely distributive because a principal ideal generated by a \(\vee\)-prime is completely \(\vee\)-prime.

thm-7-2-31.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-2-31}{Theorem 7.2.31} A lattice \(V\) is isomorphic to the lattice of compact-open subsets of an algebraic bc-domain if and only if it has a least element, each element of \(V\) is the supremum of finitely many \(\vee\)-primes, and the set of \(\vee\)-primes plus least element is closed under finite infima.

def-7-3-1.tex:
\leanmarker{def-7-3-1}{Definition 7.3.1} A coherent algebraic prelocale \(A\) is a preordered algebra with two binary operations \(\vee\) and \(\wedge\), two nullary operations \(0\) and \(1\), and a unary predicate \(C\) on \(A\), such that \(a\vee b\) is a supremum for \(\{a,b\}\), \(a\wedge b\) is an infimum for \(\{a,b\}\), \(0\) is least, and \(1\) is largest. The preorder is denoted by \(\preceq\), with associated equivalence \(\approx\). The predicate \(C(a)\) holds exactly when \(a\) is \(\vee\)-prime, and every element of \(A\) is equivalent to a finite join of \(\vee\)-primes. Write
\[
  C(A)=\{a\in A\mid C(a)\}.
\]
A \emph{domain prelocale} is a coherent algebraic prelocale satisfying the two additional conditions from Theorem 7.2.30:
\[
\begin{array}{l}
\forall u\subseteq_{\mathrm{fin}}C(A)\ \exists v\subseteq_{\mathrm{fin}}C(A).\ u\subseteq v\ \text{ and }\ (\forall w\subseteq v\ \exists z\subseteq v.\ \bigwedge w=\bigvee z),\\[1mm]
C(1).
\end{array}
\]

prop-7-3-3.tex:
\leanmarker{prop-7-3-3}{Proposition 7.3.3} There exists a map \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket:A\to K\Omega(D)\) such that the domain prelocale \(A\) is a localic description of the bifinite domain \(D\) if and only if \(\operatorname{spec}(A)\) and \(D\) are isomorphic.

\textit{Proof sketch.} A pre-isomorphism yields an isomorphism \(\operatorname{spec}(A)\to D\) by composing \(\operatorname{spec}(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket)^{-1}\) with the inverse of the unit \(\eta\). Conversely, the unit \(\epsilon:A\to K\Omega(\operatorname{spec}(A))\) is surjective, order-preserving, and order-reflecting by Proposition 7.2.4.

thm-7-3-4.tex: \leanmarker{thm-7-3-4}{Theorem 7.3.4} The category of domain prelocales and join-approximable relations is dually equivalent to the category of bifinite domains and Scott-continuous functions.

prop-7-3-6.tex:
\leanmarker{prop-7-3-6}{Proposition 7.3.6} If \(A\) is a sub-prelocale of \(B\), then the following maps define an embedding-projection pair between \(\operatorname{spec}(A)\) and \(\operatorname{spec}(B)\):
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
e:\operatorname{spec}(A)\to\operatorname{spec}(B), & e(F)=\uparrow_B(F),\\[1mm]
p:\operatorname{spec}(B)\to\operatorname{spec}(A), & p(F)=F\cap A.
\end{array}
\]
\textit{Proof sketch.} Directed joins of prime filters are directed unions, so both maps are continuous. The identity \(p\circ e=\operatorname{id}\) follows because the preorder on \(A\) is the restriction of that on \(B\), and \(e\circ p\sqsubseteq\operatorname{id}\) needs no special assumptions. The main point is well-definedness: the filter property follows from the inherited operations and preorder, and primeness follows because the \(\vee\)-prime elements of \(A\) are precisely the \(\vee\)-prime elements of \(B\) lying in \(A\).

cor-7-3-7.tex:
\leanmarker{cor-7-3-7}{Corollary 7.3.7} Assume that \(A\) is a localic description of \(D\) via \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket_A\), that \(B\) describes \(E\) via \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket_B\), and that \(A\preccurlyeq B\). Then the following defines an embedding of \(D\) into \(E\): if \(c\in K(D)\), \(a\in C(A)\), \(\llbracket a\rrbracket_A^0=\uparrow c\), and \(\llbracket a\rrbracket_B^0=\uparrow d\), then \(e(c)=d\).

The proof identifies this embedding as \(\tau_B\circ e'\circ\tau_A^{-1}\), where \(e'\) is the embedding \(\operatorname{spec}(A)\to\operatorname{spec}(B)\) from Proposition 7.3.6.

lemma-7-3-8.tex:
\leanmarker{lemma-7-3-8}{Lemma 7.3.8} The Scott topology on the function space \([D\to D']\), for bifinite domains \(D\) and \(D'\), equals the compact-open topology.

\textit{Proof sketch.} If \(A\subseteq D\) is compact and \(O\subseteq D'\) is open, then \((A\Rightarrow O)=\{f\mid f(A)\subseteq O\}\) is Scott-open: compactness of \(A\) reduces directed suprema pointwise to finitely many inverse images. Conversely, every Scott-open neighborhood of a function contains a compact-open neighborhood obtained from idempotent deflations on \(D\) and \(D'\).

lemma-7-3-9.tex:
\leanmarker{lemma-7-3-9}{Lemma 7.3.9} Let \(D\) and \(D'\) be bifinite, and let \(A\subseteq D\) and \(A'\subseteq D'\) be compact-open. Then
\[
  (A\Rightarrow A')=\{f\in[D\to D']\mid f(A)\subseteq A'\}
\]
is compact-open in \([D\to D']\).

\textit{Proof sketch.} By Lemma 7.3.8 this set is open. Bifiniteness supplies idempotent deflations \(g_n\) on \(D\) and \(g'_m\) on \(D'\) with \(A=\uparrow g_n(A)\) and \(A'=\uparrow g'_m(A')\). The induced idempotent deflation \(G_{nm}(f)=g'_m\circ f\circ g_n\) satisfies \((A\Rightarrow A')=\uparrow G_{nm}(A\Rightarrow A')\).

thm-7-3-10.tex:
\leanmarker{thm-7-3-10}{Theorem 7.3.10} Let \(A\) and \(B\) be domain prelocales. Then
\[
  [\operatorname{spec}(A)\to\operatorname{spec}(B)]\cong \operatorname{spec}([A\to B]),
\]
and this isomorphism is natural with respect to the sub-prelocale relation.

lemma-7-3-11.tex:
\leanmarker{lemma-7-3-11}{Lemma 7.3.11} If \(D\) is a bifinite domain and \(O\) is compact-open in \(D\), then the following are compact-open subsets of \(P^P(D)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
  A(O) &= \{L\in\operatorname{Lens}(D)\mid L\subseteq O\},\\
  E(O) &= \{L\in\operatorname{Lens}(D)\mid L\cap O\ne\emptyset\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Moreover, as \(O\) ranges over all compact-open subsets of \(D\), the sets \(A(O)\) and \(E(O)\) form a base for the Scott topology on \(P^P(D)\).

\textit{Proof sketch.} For compact-open \(O\), choose an idempotent deflation \(d\) with \(O=\uparrow d(O)\). Its lifted deflation \(\hat d=P^P(d)\) makes both \(A(O)\) and \(E(O)\) compact-open. A compact lens \(K=\operatorname{Cx}(u)\), with finite \(u\subseteq K(D)\), has upper set expressible as \(A(\uparrow u)\cap\bigcap_{c\in u}E(\uparrow c)\).

def-7-3-12.tex:
\leanmarker{def-7-3-12}{Definition 7.3.12} Let \(A\) be a domain prelocale which is a localic description of the bifinite domain \(D\). The Plotkin powerlocale \(P^P(A)\) over \(A\) is the term algebra over the generators
\[
  G_P=\{\Box a\mid a\in A\}\cup\{\Diamond a\mid a\in A\},
\]
with interpretation \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket:P^P(A)\to K\Omega(P^P(D))\) defined on generators by
\[
  \llbracket\Box a\rrbracket=A(\llbracket a\rrbracket),
  \qquad
  \llbracket\Diamond a\rrbracket=E(\llbracket a\rrbracket),
\]
and extended to \(P^P(A)\) as a lattice homomorphism. The preorder and \(C\)-predicate are given by the rules displayed below.

thm-7-3-13.tex:
\leanmarker{thm-7-3-13}{Theorem 7.3.13} Let \(A\) be a domain prelocale. Then
\[
  P^P(\operatorname{spec}(A))\cong \operatorname{spec}(P^P(A)),
\]
and this isomorphism is natural with respect to the sub-prelocale relation. The Hoare and Smyth powerdomain prelocales are obtained by eliding the generators and rules referring to \(\Box\), respectively \(\Diamond\).

thm-7-3-14.tex:
\leanmarker{thm-7-3-14}{Theorem 7.3.14} If
\[
  A_0\preccurlyeq A_1\preccurlyeq A_2\preccurlyeq\cdots
\]
is a chain of domain prelocales, then
\[
  \operatorname{spec}\Bigl(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}A_n\Bigr)
  \cong
  \operatorname{bilim}(\operatorname{spec}(A_n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}.
\]

thm-7-3-15.tex:
\leanmarker{thm-7-3-15}{Theorem 7.3.15} If \(\rho_L\) and \(\rho_D\) are environments such that, for every \(X\in TV\), the domain prelocale \(\rho_L(X)\) is a localic description of \(\rho_D(X)\), then for every type expression \(\sigma\), \(\mathcal{I}_L(\sigma;\rho_L)\) is a localic description of \(\mathcal{I}_D(\sigma;\rho_D)\). Equivalently,
\[
  \operatorname{spec}(\mathcal{I}_L(\sigma;\rho_L))
  \cong
  \mathcal{I}_D(\sigma;\rho_D).
\]

thm-7-3-16.tex:
\leanmarker{thm-7-3-16}{Theorem 7.3.16} If \(\sigma\) is a closed type expression, then
\[
  \operatorname{spec}(\mathcal{L}(\sigma))\cong \mathcal{I}_D(\sigma).
\]
This is the closed-type instance of Theorem 7.3.15.

thm-7-3-17.tex:
\leanmarker{thm-7-3-17}{Theorem 7.3.17} The language of properties is decidable.

\textit{Proof sketch.} For \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{1})\) only combinations of \(\mathrm{true}\) and \(\mathrm{false}\) occur. For composite types, every expression in \(\mathcal{L}(\sigma)\) can effectively be transformed into a finite disjunction of \(\vee\)-primes. Soundness and completeness identify these \(\vee\)-primes with the explicit prime expressions produced by the construction rules, and the preorder between them reduces by structural induction on \(\sigma\) to the preorder in \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{1})\).

thm-7-3-18.tex:
\leanmarker{thm-7-3-18}{Theorem 7.3.18} The domain logic is sound and complete. In formula form,
\[
  \forall M,\Gamma,\phi.\quad
  \Gamma\vdash M:\phi
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \Gamma\vDash M:\phi.
\]

p106-b6.tex: Distributivity becomes central when we pass from domains to lattices of open sets. It is closely connected with approximation. To keep notation distinct, spaces will ultimately be domains, while their open-set lattices use lattice notation such as \(\le\), \(\vee\), and \(\wedge\).

p108-b1.tex: The relation \(\lll\) is defined like the order of approximation, except that arbitrary subsets replace directed subsets. The fundamental results for approximation have corresponding versions for \(\lll\), and Raney's theorem characterizes complete distributivity in these terms.

p108-b4.tex: We next study generation by meets, but only from distinguished elements. The definition is stated slightly more generally than needed later.

p109-b15.tex: A topology \(\tau\) on a set \(X\) is an ordered set under inclusion, and in fact a complete lattice because arbitrary unions exist. If \(f:X\to Y\) is continuous, inverse image sends opens of \(Y\) to opens of \(X\), preserving arbitrary joins and finite meets. Thus a space determines its frame of opens, and continuous maps act contravariantly by inverse image.

p110-b14.tex: A point of a topological space can be described by its filter of open neighbourhoods, by the complement of its closure, or by a continuous map from the one-point space. Translating this to lattices, a point of a complete lattice is represented by a completely prime filter, equivalently by a frame homomorphism to the two-element lattice \(2\).

p111-b3.tex: The construction is symmetric. In a space, a point \(x\) belongs to an open \(O\) when \(x\in O\). In \(\operatorname{pt}(L)\), a point \(F\) belongs to the basic open \(O_x\) when \(x\in F\). A frame homomorphism \(h:K\to L\) induces a continuous map \(\operatorname{pt}(h):\operatorname{pt}(L)\to\operatorname{pt}(K)\) by inverse image of filters. Thus \(\operatorname{pt}\) is a contravariant functor from complete lattices to topological spaces.

p111-b5.tex:
Every space \(X\) maps to the space of points of its open-set lattice by
\[
  \eta_X(x)=\mathcal F_x,
\]
where \(\mathcal F_x\) is the filter of open neighbourhoods of \(x\). This map is continuous and natural. Conversely, for a complete lattice \(L\), the map
\[

p121-b9.tex:
Having established the duality between algebraic domains and their lattices of compact-open subsets, we can ask how far domain theory can be carried out through these lattices. For a bifinite domain \(D\), the lifted domain is handled by adjoining a new top element:
\[
  K\Omega(D_{\perp}) = K\Omega(D)^{\top}.
\]
Coalesced sums behave similarly:
\[
  K\Omega(D\oplus E)=(K\Omega(D)\setminus\{D\})\times (K\Omega(E)\setminus\{E\})\cup\{D\oplus E\}.
\]
The first real difficulty is the cartesian product: although each compact-open subset of \(D\times E\) is a finite union of products of compact-open subsets in the factors, there is no simple uniqueness criterion for such unions.

\subsubsection*{7.3.5 Recursive domain equations}
Suppose
\[
A_0\preccurlyeq A_1\preccurlyeq A_2\preccurlyeq\cdots
\]
is a chain of domain prelocales and each \(A_n\) describes a bifinite domain \(D_n\). \[
  \llbracket a\rrbracket=l_m(\llbracket a\rrbracket_{A_m}),
\]
where \(m\) is chosen with \(a\in A_m\). This is independent of \(m\): if \(m\le k\), then
\[
  \llbracket a\rrbracket_{A_k}=e_{km}(\llbracket a\rrbracket_{A_m}),
  \qquad
  l_k(\llbracket a\rrbracket_{A_k})=l_m(\llbracket a\rrbracket_{A_m}).
\]
Soundness, prime generation, completeness, definability, and naturality follow from the corresponding finite stages. For naturality, if \(B=\bigcup B_n\) is a second chain and \(A_n\preccurlyeq B_n\), the embedding \(e:D\to E\) satisfies for \(a\in C(A)\):

\begin{aligned}
e(\llbracket a\rrbracket_A^0)

\end{aligned}
\]

Recall that a lattice \(L\) is distributive if, for all \(x,y,z\in L\),
\[
  x\wedge (y\vee z) = (x\wedge y)\vee (x\wedge z).
\]
For complete distributivity, if \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) is a family of sets, write
\(f:I\overset{\odot}{\longrightarrow}\bigcup_i A_i\) when \(f(i)\in A_i\) for every \(i\in I\). Complete distributivity is expressed by
\[
  \bigwedge_{i\in I}\bigvee A_i
  =
  \bigvee_{f:I\overset{\odot}{\longrightarrow}\bigcup_i A_i}
    \bigwedge_{i\in I} f(i).
\]

p107-b10.tex: The proof checks that the right-hand supremum is directed. If \(x\) approximates the left-hand side, then for each \(i\in I\) there is \(a_i\in A_i\) with \(x\le a_i\); choosing these \(a_i\) gives \(x\le\bigwedge_i f(i)\). Conversely, for a fixed \(x\), take all directed sets \(A\) with \(x\le\bigvee{}^{\uparrow}A\). The displayed equality gives approximants \(\bigwedge_i f(i)\), and directedness yields the required approximation of \(x\).

p109-b1.tex:
A dual statement holds for lattices which are \(\vee\)-generated by \(\vee\)-prime elements. The proof uses a \(\wedge\)-prime element \(p\) above the right-hand side of the first equation: for every choice function \(f\), primeness gives an index \(m_f\) with \(p\ge f(m_f)\). The set of all such selected values must cover at least one \(A_m\); otherwise a contrary choice function gives a contradiction. Thus \(p\) is above \(\bigvee A_m\) for some \(m\), and hence above \(\bigwedge_m\bigvee A_m\). The second equation is similar. The first equation is equivalent to the frame distributivity law
\[
  x\wedge\bigvee_{i\in I}y_i = \bigvee_{i\in I}(x\wedge y_i),
\]
which uses arbitrary joins and finite meets.

The moral is that we must allow multiple representations of compact-open subsets. Instead of lattices we study certain preordered structures. This may first look like an unwanted complication, but it makes the programme smoother: lattices are determined by either their order structure or their algebraic structure, while this equivalence no longer holds in the preordered case. We therefore mention both preorder and lattice operations, and make \(\vee\)-primeness explicit in the axiomatization.

p124-b9.tex: Remember that \(C(K\Omega(D))\) consists exactly of those compact-open subsets of the form \(\uparrow c\), for \(c\in K(D)\). The inclusion order between such principal filters is dual to the usual order on \(K(D)\). We now lift the pre-isomorphism to the domain level. Instead of applying ideal completion to the pre-isomorphism between \(C(A)^{op}\) and \(K(D)\), we use Stone duality and apply \(\operatorname{spec}\) to \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket\). This yields an isomorphism between \(\operatorname{spec}(A)\) and \(\operatorname{spec}(K\Omega(D))\).

p125-b1.tex:
Composed with the inverse of the unit \(\eta\), the spectrum map gives the isomorphism
\[
\tau:\operatorname{spec}(A)\to D.
\]
The corresponding triangle is
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\operatorname{spec}(A) & \xrightarrow{\tau} & D \\
\operatorname{spec}(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket)^{-1}\downarrow & & \nearrow\eta^{-1} \\
\operatorname{spec}(K\Omega(D)) & &
\end{array}
\]

p125-b8.tex: It is useful to know how \(\tau\) behaves on compact elements of \(\operatorname{spec}(A)\). These are the filters generated by \(\vee\)-prime elements. If \(F=\uparrow a\) with \(a\in C(A)\), then \(\tau(F)\) is the compact element \(c\) of \(D\) which is least in the compact-open subset \(\llbracket a\rrbracket^0\).

p126-b12.tex: The lower part of the diagram compares compact elements of \(F_T(D,D')\) with the \(\vee\)-prime compact-open elements of \(K\Omega(F_T(D,D'))\).

p127-b1.tex:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{The set-up.} Fix a construction \(T\) on bifinite domains, with associated functor \(F_T\). For a binary construction we assume we understand \(F_T(D,D')\), its compact elements \(K(F_T(D,D'))\), the compact-open lattice \(K\Omega(F_T(D,D'))\), and the \(\vee\)-prime elements \(C(K\Omega(F_T(D,D')))\). The latter are exactly the principal filters \(\uparrow c\), for compact \(c\), ordered by inclusion, which is dual to the usual order on compact elements.
\item \textbf{The goal.} Given localic descriptions \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket_A:A\to K\Omega(D)\) and \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket_{A'}:A'\to K\Omega(D')\), construct a domain prelocale \(T(A,A')\) which describes \(F_T(D,D')\).
\item \textbf{Definition of \(T(A,A')\).} Choose generators \(G_T\), take the term algebra over \(G_T\) for \(\vee,\wedge,0,1\), define an interpretation \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket:G_T\to K\Omega(F_T(D,D'))\), extend it homomorphically, and then impose axioms/rules governing the preorder and primeness predicate.
\item \textbf{Soundness.} Show that the axioms and rules translate through \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket\) to valid compact-open facts. This also gives a restricted map \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket^0:C(T(A,A'))\to C(K\Omega(F_T(D,D')))\).
\item \textbf{Prime generation.} Prove that every element of \(T(A,A')\) can be transformed into a finite supremum of \(\vee\)-prime expressions. This gives the remaining structural properties of \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket\) from \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket^0\).
\end{enumerate}

p128-b2.tex:
\textit{Proof of completeness.} Let \(a,b\in T(A,A')\) and assume \(\llbracket a\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket b\rrbracket\). By prime generation, write
\[
  a\approx a_1\vee\cdots\vee a_n,
  \qquad
  b\approx b_1\vee\cdots\vee b_m,
\]
with all \(a_i,b_j\) \(\vee\)-prime. Soundness keeps the interpretation unchanged, and each \(\llbracket a_i\rrbracket\) and \(\llbracket b_j\rrbracket\) is of the form \(\uparrow c_i\), respectively \(\uparrow d_j\), for compact elements of \(F_T(D,D')\). Inclusion in \(K\Omega(F_T(D,D'))\) gives
\[
  \forall i\ \exists j.\ \uparrow c_i\subseteq\uparrow d_j,
\]
which completeness for \(\vee\)-primes pulls back to \(\forall i\ \exists j.\ a_i\preceq b_j\). Hence \(a\preceq b\) in every preordered lattice.

\begin{enumerate}
\setcounter{enumi}{8}
\item \textbf{Definability.} Surjectivity of \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket\) follows from surjectivity of \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket^0\), since compact-open subsets in an algebraic domain are finite unions of compactly generated principal filters.
\item \textbf{Well-definedness.} The preorder and primeness predicate on \(T(A,A')\) are preserved and reflected by \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket\), so \(T(A,A')\) satisfies the domain-prelocale conditions.
\item \textbf{Stone-duality.} The pre-isomorphism \(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket\) lifts to an isomorphism \(\tau:\operatorname{spec}(T(A,A'))\to F_T(D,D')\).
\end{enumerate}

p128-b3.tex:
The Stone-duality step is represented by the triangle
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\operatorname{spec}(T(A,A')) & \xrightarrow{\tau} & F_T(D,D') \\
\operatorname{spec}(\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket)^{-1}\downarrow & & \nearrow\eta^{-1} \\
\operatorname{spec}(K\Omega(F_T(D,D'))) & &
\end{array}
\]

p128-b5.tex:
So much for the correspondence on the object level. We also need compatibility with the sub-prelocale relation and the isomorphism \(\tau\). Suppose that \(B\) and \(B'\) are localic descriptions of bifinite domains \(E\) and \(E'\), with \(A\preccurlyeq B\) and \(A'\preccurlyeq B'\). Corollary 7.3.7 gives embeddings \(e:D\to E\) and \(e':D'\to E'\). Proposition 5.2.6 gives an embedding \(F_T(e,e') : F_T(D,D')\to F_T(E,E')\), preserving compact elements, and hence a monotone restriction
\[
  F_T(e,e')^0:K(F_T(D,D'))\to K(F_T(E,E')).
\]

p129-b1.tex:
For both \(T(A,A')\) and \(T(B,B')\) there are diagrams of the kind used at the beginning of this subsection. Connecting their lower-left corners by \(F_T(e,e')^0\) gives a map
\[
  i:C(K\Omega(F_T(D,D')))\to C(K\Omega(F_T(E,E'))).
\]
Our construction makes \(C(T(A,A'))\subseteq C(T(B,B'))\), so the upper-left corners are connected by inclusion.

\textbf{12. Naturality.} We show that
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
C(T(A,A')) & \subseteq & C(T(B,B')) \\
\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket^0_{T(A,A')}\downarrow & & \downarrow\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket^0_{T(B,B')} \\
C(K\Omega(F_T(D,D'))) & \xrightarrow{i} & C(K\Omega(F_T(E,E')))
\end{array}
\]
commutes. Elementwise, if \(a\in C(T(A,A'))\), \(\llbracket a\rrbracket^0_{T(A,A')}=\uparrow c\), and \(\llbracket a\rrbracket^0_{T(B,B')}=\uparrow d\), then \(F_T(e,e')^0(c)=d\).

\textbf{13. Monotonicity.} We show \(T(A,A')\preccurlyeq T(B,B')\). The carrier inclusion and inherited axioms/rules are immediate from the construction. If \(a,a'\in C(T(A,A'))\) and \(a\preceq a'\) holds in \(T(B,B')\), correctness gives \(\uparrow d\subseteq\uparrow d'\), hence \(d\sqsubseteq d'\). Naturality gives \(F_T(e,e')^0(c)=d\) and \(F_T(e,e')^0(c')=d'\); since embeddings are order-reflecting, \(c\sqsubseteq c'\), and completeness yields \(a\preceq a'\) in \(T(A,A')\). The predicate \(C\) is restricted in the same way.

\textbf{14. Least prelocale.} Correctness of the construction gives \(\mathbf{1}\preccurlyeq T(A,A')\).

\textbf{15. Naturality of \(\tau\).} For the embedding \(I:\operatorname{spec}(T(A,A'))\to\operatorname{spec}(T(B,B'))\), the diagram
\[
\begin{array}{ccc}
\operatorname{spec}(T(A,A')) & \xrightarrow{I} & \operatorname{spec}(T(B,B')) \\
\tau_A\downarrow & & \downarrow\tau_B \\
F_T(D,D') & \xrightarrow{F_T(e,e')} & F_T(E,E')
\end{array}
\]
commutes. It suffices to check compact elements: a compact filter generated by \(a\in C(T(A,A'))\) is sent by \(\tau_A\) to the compact element generating \(\llbracket a\rrbracket^0_{T(A,A')}\), while \(I(F)\) is generated by the same term in \(T(B,B')\); Step 12 identifies the two resulting compact elements.

\]

p131-b3.tex: All index sets are finite, so the displayed meets and joins remain in the term algebra over \(G_{\to}\). The use of the \(C\)-predicate in \((\to-\vee-r)\) is essential, and distributivity is enforced explicitly. To illustrate Step 5, suppose \(\llbracket a\rrbracket_A\) has the form \(\uparrow c\cup\uparrow d\) and \(\llbracket a'\rrbracket_{A'}\) has the form \(\uparrow c'\cup\uparrow d'\). The term \((a\to a')\) is transformed by \((\to-\preceq)\), \((\to-\vee-l)\), \((\to-\vee-r)\), and distributivity into a finite disjunction of conjunctions such as \((c\to c')\wedge(d\to d')\). If \(a,b\) are \(\vee\)-prime terms with \(\llbracket a\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket b\rrbracket\), then their normal forms are joinable families \(\bigwedge_{i\in I}(a_i\to a'_i)\) and \(\bigwedge_{j\in J}(b_j\to b'_j)\). Lemma 4.2.3 gives
\[
  \forall i\in I\ \exists j\in J.\quad \llbracket b_j\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket a_i\rrbracket\ \text{ and }\ \llbracket a'_i\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket b'_j\rrbracket,

The Plotkin powerdomain \(P^P(D)\) of a bifinite domain is represented by lenses ordered by the Egli-Milner order. Its compact elements are convex closures of finite nonempty subsets of \(K(D)\). Compact-open subsets are less direct than in the Hoare or Smyth cases because one half of the Egli-Milner order refers to closed lower sets. The useful observations are the two families below.

For Step 5, generation by \(\vee\)-primes, first put a term in disjunctive normal form. It suffices to handle
\[
  \bigwedge_{i\in I}\Box a_i\wedge\bigwedge_{j\in J}\Diamond b_j.
\]
Using \((\Box-\wedge)\), pack the \(\Box\)-generators into \(\Box a\), and by (D2) assume each \(b_j\preceq a\). After decomposing each \(b_j\) into \(\vee\)-primes and distributing, one reaches terms
\[
  \Box a\wedge\bigwedge_{j=1}^m\Diamond d_j,
  \qquad d_j\in C(A).
\]
Writing \(a\) as a join of \(\vee\)-primes \(c_i\) and adjoining the \(d_j\)'s gives
\[
  \Box(c_1\vee\cdots\vee c_n\vee d_1\vee\cdots\vee d_m)
  \wedge\bigwedge_{j=1}^m\Diamond d_j.
\]
Further applications of (D1) split this into \(\vee\)-prime pieces indexed by subsets of \(\{c_1,\ldots,c_n\}\).

p135-b5.tex: One application of (D1), followed by distributivity, separates the term into two alternatives: one omits \(c_1\), and the other adds \(\Diamond c_1\). Iterating over \(c_1,\ldots,c_n\) yields the family of \(\vee\)-prime expressions required by rule \((P-C)\).
